newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Franco-German differences papered over in EMU deal.
newsitem.headline: Franco-German differences papered over in EMU deal.

text.p: EU finance ministers have once again rescued Europe's single currency plans from a serious setback, but the potential fallout from their agreement on jobs and fiscal discipline may open up a new set of uncertainties.

After a heated row between Bonn and Paris over how to tackle Europe's high unemployment rate, the ministers reached a compromise that seems to appease France and allows the bloc to sign a critical pact on fiscal discipline within EMU.
"We have reached complete agreement on the stability pact and the resolution for growth and employment," Dutch Finance Minister Gerrit Zalm told reporters.

The employment accord, a non-binding political resolution that will include a role for the European Investment Bank, comes in response to the new French government's demands that more should be done to help the 18 million unemployed in the EU.
For some observers the important issue of this episode is how much political capital has been spent by Germany and France in mending their differences and putting the euro first.
"The key question is how much tension this process has created," said Tim Stewart, global currency strategist at Morgan Stanley.
With Germany and France the two main engines behind economic and political integration, a continued close relationship is considered essential for EMU's good fortune.

But since the new French government took over the reigns of power there has been a noticeable rise in tensions between the two powers, with Germany seeing its vision of the single currency gradually clipped at the edges.

Gone are all expectations that the Maastricht Treaty criteria for entry into the euro will be applied in a strict fashion. Flexibility is now the common buzz word, leading most analysts to expect a soft euro, or one with many members.
"One must assume that EMU goes ahead and with a broad group," Stewart added.

Part of this outcome is due to Germany's own difficulties in bringing its public finances under control. Bonn faces a huge revenue shortfall in this year's budget with no clear plan of how it will be reversed.
As a result, Germany has lost virtually all the moral authority it once had in lecturing others on their budgetary slackness.

The debate within Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling coalition over the 1997 deficit outlook -- and for Germany's longer-term health, tax reform -- has led to the most severe political crisis in his nearly 15 years in office.

Equally important is public opinion. Analysts say that as it becomes clear the euro will be purchased at any price, German public resistance to the project could grow, making life for Kohl's foot soldiers that much more difficult.
"You still have the question of what happens inside Germany and I'm not so sure how that is going to play out," said a London-based economist.

Meanwhile for France, there is undoubtedly a great sense of satisfaction in having moved the debate over EMU away from the Germany's obsession with monetary and fiscal rigour and towards the concerns many Europeans have with jobs and security.

Yet what was accomplished in Amsterdam still needs to be sold in France, and a critical first test comes on June 19 when Prime Minister Lionel Jospin presents his economic policy programme to the National Assembly.

Whether the French electorate will be satisfied with its government's accomplishments in Amsterdam is another question mark, and there were hints on Monday that Paris would try to push its new found European influence even further.
"This is only the beginning. We have begun to reverse the trend, we have loosened the noose," said a French government spokesman.
